query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy, the favorable strength–ductility balance under dynamic (varying temperature/strain rate) conditions is governed by a transition in the dominant plastic deformation mechanism. At lower temperatures and/or high strain rates, the suppression of Co leads to a reduced propensity for deformation twinning and instead promotes a dislocation‐dominated slip regime that, upon accumulating stress, triggers an earlier onset of dynamic recrystallization. In contrast, at higher temperatures and/or lower strain rates, thermally activated dislocation climb and recovery become dominant, leading to controlled softening. This transition explains the alloy’s dynamic behavior relative to the Co‐containing baseline, where twinning is more pronounced.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid‐solution, equiatomic (minus Co) FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy produced by conventional processing.
generation.intervention: Removal of Co from the canonical equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Tests performed over a wide temperature range (from cryogenic conditions up to elevated temperatures around 600 °C) and varying strain rates (from high to low rates), where the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution without precipitation.
generation.structural_mediator: Changes in the microstructural features such as the density and distribution of dislocations, twin boundaries, and dynamic recrystallized grains.
generation.mechanism: Without Co the stacking fault energy and local atomic interactions shift the balance between deformation twinning and dislocation activities. At lower temperatures/high strain rates, twinning is suppressed so that plastic deformation is mainly accommodated by dislocation glide, leading to higher stored strain energy and an earlier transition to dynamic recrystallization. At higher temperatures/low strain rates, thermally activated processes (dislocation climb and recovery) become more active, reducing flow stress while preserving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the traditional equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, the Co‐free alloy will display (a) a statistically significantly lower twin density under identical low-temperature/high strain rate conditions, (b) an earlier onset of dynamic recrystallization at elevated temperatures or lower strain rates, and (c) a distinct stress–strain response with altered work‐hardening exponents. These differences serve to balance strength and ductility by tailoring the operative plasticity mechanisms according to temperature and strain rate.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) alloy whose dynamic behavior is known to involve substantial deformation twinning and stacking fault formation under comparable testing conditions.
generation.boundary: Applicable as long as the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution (i.e., before any precipitation or phase separation occurs) and for testing conditions within the practical range (cryogenic up to around 600 °C and moderate to high strain rates).
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative shift from twinning to dislocation/recrystallization control is predicted, the precise quantitative differences (e.g., twin density, recrystallization onset stress/strain) and sensitivity to processing history remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy and one of the conventional equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy. Conduct in situ TEM mechanical tests while systematically varying temperature (e.g., from cryogenic to 600 °C) and strain rate. Quantitatively measure the evolution of dislocation structures, twin boundaries, and dynamic recrystallized grain sizes alongside macroscopic stress–strain curves.
measurements: Twin and dislocation densities (via high-resolution TEM)
Work‐hardening rate and yield strength from stress–strain curves
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co‐free alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in twin density and an earlier onset of dynamic recrystallization compared to the Co-containing alloy under matched conditions, or if its stress–strain behavior does not differ in the predicted manner, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . For centuries, constructions with high mechanical requirements have been built using steel or iron-based alloys, while titanium or aluminum have been used for light-weight constructions. In gas turbines nickel- or cobalt-based superalloys are used because of their extremely good mechanical properties and oxidation resistance over long periods of time at high temperatures. The main properties of these alloys are given by their base element, while the addition of other elements in small amounts leads to fine adjustments of a specific behavior [ [1] ].

An unconventional approach of alloy design is based not on a main element, but on a chemical composition that exhibits a large number of elements with none of them dominating. In this group one differentiates between single-phase high entropy alloys (HEA) [ [2] ] and multiphase compositionally complex alloys (CCA). Multicomponent alloys were examined first by Yeh [ [2] ] and Cantor [ [3] ]. Investigating the microstructure of alloys with different numbers of elements in equiatomic mixtures, Cantor found the five-component, equiatomic alloy Co 20 Cr 20 Fe 20 Mn 20 Ni 20 to form a single-phase solid-solution.
